t: Bullying In The Classroom: The Ultimate Guide To Stopping It
q: Bullying is the strong preying upon the weak. It can be a physical advantage or a social advantage. It can be one student or many.

Don’t wait for someone else to step in. Don’t assume that because you referred the bullying behavior to the principal or a counselor that it’s going to be taken care of. You take on the responsibility and see it through to the end.
Watch your class like a hawk. Always. Notice body language. Keep an eye on students who are socially awkward, smaller in stature, or less confident.
When you get a report of bullying, take your time gathering the facts. Take notes, interview witnesses, and open a file for documentation. Don’t be in a rush to react—and don’t overreact.
Keep the bullying student(s) in extended time-out for one week. Also, keep him (or her) with you, or under adult supervision, during recess.

The truth is, bullying rarely if ever happens in well-run classrooms. When standards of behavior are clearly communicated, when students are held accountable using an effective classroom management plan , and when the teacher is well-versed in fair, effective strategies, then students don’t bully.
Parents instinctively will do anything to protect their children. They’ll go to the ends of the earth to care for them. They’ll stand in front of anyone or anything wishing to harm them.
x: Follow up with both the bullied student and the bully—and their parents—for weeks after the incident, not just once.
Use an extended one-week time-out with a written and recited apology as the consequence for bullying behavior.
Identify quiet, isolated, or socially vulnerable students early and build trusted 'eyes and ears' among class leaders.
When an incident occurs, gather facts calmly before reacting, then separate the bully into time-out immediately.

t: How To Stem The Tide Of Student Questions
q: The most important key to managing questions is to tightly control when they may be asked. If you allow an all-day question free-for-all, which is surprisingly common, your progress through the curriculum will be a frustrating plod.
It’s best to allow for questions only during specified segments throughout the day. So at any given moment the floor will either be open to questions or it won’t.
Never answer a repeated question. It encourages students to tune you out. Instead, ask the student to check with a neighbor as soon as independent work begins.
Call on students who are sitting with their hand raised in the manner in which you modeled. Don’t respond to those who approach you, wave at you, or call out to you . Instead, enforce a consequence.

It’s important your students feel encouraged and motivated to ask questions and participate in their learning. But at the same time you’ve got to keep the pace of your classroom crisp and moving forward.
x: His central recommendation is to open designated 'question segments' tied to specific topics rather than allowing an all-day free-for-all.
Restrict questions to defined 'segments' tied to a specific topic rather than allowing them all day long.
Refuse to answer repeated questions or call-outs; redirect students to ask a neighbor or enforce a consequence.
The piece also recommends refusing to answer repeated questions or respond to call-outs, hand-waving, or students approaching out of turn, instead enforcing a consequence.
Give students post-its to jot down questions so they can let go of them until question time arrives.

t: 7 Reasons Why You Shouldn't Lecture Your Students
q: So you run out, pull Anthony off the playground, and let him have it. You give him a fire-breathing, finger-pointing, he’s-got-it-comin’ lecture, topped off with a stern, “Do you understand me?

Using words to try and convince students to behave is perhaps the number one cause of stress among teachers. And because lecturing kinda-sorta works in the short term, teachers feel encouraged to keep on doing it—despite the tension headaches.
When you lecture, you all but dare your students to argue with you . In fact, it takes a strong-willed student not to.
Your words will never carry as much weight as your actions. And the longer students are in school, the more this is true.
Simply tell the student what rule was broken, then enforce a consequence and move on to more important things—like teaching your class.
x: Opening with a vignette of a teacher pulling a student off the playground for a scolding, Linsin makes the case that lecturing misbehaving students is a counterproductive habit even though it can feel effective in the…
Lecturing feels effective short-term but is one of the biggest sources of teacher stress and burnout.
A lecture on the way to time-out can feel like a 'double consequence' to students, breeding resentment instead of reflection.
Actions consistently carry more behavioral weight with students than words ever will.
Say only what rule was broken, enforce the consequence, and move on; let accountability do the teaching.

t: How To Talk To Parents About Their Misbehaving Child ving-child/
q: Their protective instinct kicks in, their emotions flare, and in an instant you find yourself backpedaling, apologizing, and explaining away your decisions and methods.

It’s a mistake to be grave or overly serious when speaking to parents, which causes them to put up a wall of defense before you even get to the purpose of your meeting. Put them at ease from the beginning.

A common mistake teachers make is that they affect an attitude of “so what are you gonna do about it” when speaking to parents. It’s almost as if they expect parents to make sure that it doesn’t happen again.
You can and should say, “This is the behavior I’m seeing, and any behavior, like this, that interferes with learning is not allowed in this classroom.” Don’t hold back in this regard.

Your conversation with parents should last no more than five minutes. As soon as you finish explaining how you’re handling the misbehavior, say, “Thanks for your support. Call me or come see me if you have any questions.
x: Linsin addresses a common teacher fear—discussing a child's misbehavior with parents—by naming the underlying anxieties: that parents will grow defensive, question competence, or make demands.
Stay friendly and put parents at ease immediately—gravity and seriousness trigger defensiveness before you've said anything.
